# Summary: Jacek Karpiński
Jacek Karpiński (1927–2010) was a Polish engineer and computer pioneer noted for his innovative contributions despite political and institutional obstacles. After recovering from wartime injuries and completing his education, he worked at the Polish Academy of Sciences, creating significant devices such as the Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics (AAH) for improving weather forecasts, the AKAT-1—the world's first transistor-based differential equations analyzer (1959), and one of the first perceptrons based on Frank Rosenblatt's ideas (1964). He received international recognition through a UNESCO award, which enabled him to visit leading U.S. research centers and meet scientists including Claude Shannon; this period was marked by cooperation with Polish intelligence focused on gathering technological data.
Karpiński led the development of KAR-65 in 1968, then Poland's fastest computer, and is best known for designing the K-202 minicomputer (1973), notable for its use of Intel 4004 microchips and modular architecture that rivaled Western products like the PDP-11. Ultimately, only 30 K-202 units were produced due to institutional sabotage, withdrawal of support, and political disfavor. After leaving computer research, Karpiński had varied careers abroad and at home, including work for Nagra recorders in Switzerland and unsuccessful business ventures. He was honored with the Officer's and Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta for his engineering achievements. Controversies later emerged regarding his role as a secret informant for Communist intelligence and debates over the real scale and global significance of his technical legacy.
